lead: This unit teaches how a sensor is described in numbers: what it measures, what it puts out, how wrong it can be, and how fast it follows a change. After it you can read a sensor datasheet, run a simple calibration, compute accuracy, precision, sensitivity and linearity, model a sensor as zero, first or second order, and put an uncertainty on a measured value.
about: The unit starts with what a sensor is and how sensors are grouped, then asks why each one works — the physical law that turns a temperature, force or light level into a resistance, capacitance or emf. Chapter 1.3 ties every reading to agreed units, standards and a calibration traceable to the SI. Chapters 1.4 and 1.5 turn that into the numbers an engineer quotes: accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity and linearity for a steady input, and time constant, natural frequency and damping for a changing one. Chapter 1.6 closes the loop: how errors arise, how repeated readings combine into a mean and a standard deviation, and how much of the final answer you can trust.

chapters.idea: Every sensor either makes its own electrical energy from the measurand (active) or needs an external supply whose current it modifies (passive), and this single fact decides its wiring and signal conditioning.
chapters.depth: Define sensor, transducer, actuator and inverse transducer, and show the general input-output chain: measurand → sensing element → variable-conversion element → variable-manipulation element → output. Some syllabi call this the general input-output configuration of a measurement system. Give the major classification axes: by energy source (active/self-generating vs passive/externally energised — some syllabi use those longer names instead of active and passive), by output form (analog vs digital), by physical principle (resistive, inductive, capacitive, piezoelectric, thermoelectric, photoelectric, Hall effect), by contact (contact vs non-contact), and by application. Active examples: thermocouple, piezoelectric crystal, photovoltaic cell, tachogenerator. Passive examples: RTD, thermistor, strain gauge, potentiometer, LVDT, photoconductive cell, capacitive sensor. State the wiring consequence in one line: an active sensor is a voltage or charge source and needs a high-impedance load; a passive sensor is a variable impedance and needs excitation plus a bridge or divider. Keep it a survey, not a circuit course.
chapters.example: Classify each device as active or passive and justify with one number. (a) A Pt100 RTD of 100.0 Ω at 0 °C run at 1 mA excitation: power dissipated = I²R = (1×10⁻³)² × 100 = 1×10⁻⁴ W = 0.10 mW, so the RTD is passive and the excitation sets its self-heating. (b) A piezoelectric accelerometer giving 12 mV per g with no supply — active. (c) A photodiode in photovoltaic mode giving 0.45 V in sunlight — active. (d) The same photodiode in photoconductive mode with 5 V reverse bias — passive, because the bias current changes with light.
chapters.trap: The most common error is marking a photodiode 'passive' by habit. It is active in photovoltaic mode and passive in photoconductive mode. Second trap: mixing up a sensing element and a transducer — the diaphragm is a sensing element, the capacitive pressure transducer is the whole device with its output terminals.
chapters.prereq: Basic electrical circuits: Ohm's law, voltage and current sources, power P = VI = I²R.
chapters.leave: Construction and circuits of potentiometers, strain gauges, RTDs, thermistors and thermocouples to Unit 2; LVDT, inductive and capacitive transducer design to Unit 3; piezoelectric and Hall effect detail to Unit 4; signal conditioning and bridges to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A sensor is a small physics experiment: a known physical law converts the measurand into a change of resistance, capacitance, inductance or emf that we can measure electrically.
chapters.depth: Organise the physical principles by energy domain (mechanical, thermal, electrical, magnetic, radiant, chemical) and give the working law for each family with the symbols defined: resistance R = ρL/A and its change with length, area and resistivity; capacitance C = εA/d for parallel plates; inductance of a coil and Faraday's law e = −dΦ/dt; the Seebeck effect (temperature difference gives an emf); the piezoresistive effect ΔR/R = GF·ε, where GF is the gauge factor and ε is strain; the piezoelectric effect (stress gives charge, q = d·F, with d the charge coefficient); the photoelectric effect (photovoltaic emf and photoconductive change of resistance); the Hall effect V_H = K_H·I·B/t; magnetostriction and magneto-elastic change of permeability; humidity sensing by a hygroscopic layer changing resistance or capacitance. For each, state the measurand, the intermediate variable and the electrical output, and one typical application. Also cover electric charge, field and potential (E = V/d, Q = CV) because capacitive sensors depend on them. Mention that the same law can serve two measurands (a capacitor senses displacement or humidity), so the packaging decides.

figure.title: One sensing path
figure.aria: A downward chain from the stimulus through the sensing element and the governing physical law to a change in an electrical parameter and finally to a readable electrical output.

chapters.example: A capacitive pressure sensor has two plates of area A = 25 mm² separated by d = 0.10 mm of air (εr ≈ 1, ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m). Find C, then find C when pressure pushes the gap down by 0.01 mm. C = ε₀A/d = (8.854×10⁻¹² × 25×10⁻⁶) / (1.0×10⁻⁴) = 2.21×10⁻¹² F = 2.21 pF. New gap = 0.09 mm gives C = 2.46 pF, a change of +0.25 pF or +11.1 % for a 10 % gap change. Small-signal sensitivity at the start: |dC/dd| = ε₀A/d² = C/d = 2.21 pF / 100 µm = 0.022 pF/µm.
chapters.trap: Do not confuse piezoresistive with piezoelectric. Piezoresistive changes resistance under strain and works for steady loads; piezoelectric makes charge under stress and cannot hold a steady reading without charge leakage. Second trap: the capacitance formula is non-linear in d, so a 10 % gap change gives about 11 % capacitance change, not 10 %.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for the classification vocabulary. Basic electricity and magnetism: charge, field, potential, Ohm's law, Faraday's law.
chapters.leave: Gauge factor, bridge circuits and strain gauge construction to Units 2 and 6; thermocouple laws and cold-junction compensation to Unit 2; capacitive and inductive transducer designs to Unit 3; piezoelectric, Hall effect and optical detail to Unit 4; MEMS and micro-fabrication of these principles to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A number from a sensor means nothing until it is expressed in agreed units and compared against a standard of known accuracy, and that chain of comparison is what calibration records.
chapters.depth: Revise the SI base units (metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela) and the derived units a sensor datasheet uses (volt, ohm, farad, pascal, newton, hertz, degree Celsius). Show unit conversion and dimensional checks in one or two steps. Explain the hierarchy of standards: international standards held at BIPM, national primary standards (in India the national metrology institute, NPL, New Delhi), secondary or reference standards maintained by calibration laboratories, and working standards used on a plant floor. Define traceability: an unbroken chain of calibrations each with a stated uncertainty, ending at a primary standard. Define calibration as comparing the instrument output with a known input from a standard and recording the result; distinguish it from verification (checking it is within limits) and from adjustment (zero and span trims). Describe a static calibration procedure: hold other inputs constant, apply five to ten inputs over the range going up and coming down, record output, fit the end-point or least-squares straight line, and write the certificate (range, sensitivity, zero offset, hysteresis, uncertainty, conditions). Some syllabi call the standard used for the comparison a 'reference standard' rather than a secondary standard — both names are fine.

figure.aria: A five-layer ladder from the SI base units at the top down through primary, secondary and working standards to the sensor being calibrated, with accuracy falling as you go down.

chapters.example: A 0–200 kPa pressure sensor is calibrated against a dead-weight tester. Applied pressure (kPa): 0, 50, 100, 150, 200. Output (V): 0.02, 1.01, 1.98, 3.02, 4.00. End-point sensitivity = (4.00 − 0.02) / (200 − 0) = 0.0199 V/kPa ≈ 19.9 mV/kPa. Zero offset = 0.02 V. Ideal at 100 kPa = 0.02 + 0.0199 × 100 = 2.01 V, measured 1.98 V, so the largest deviation from the end-point line is 0.03 V = 0.03/4.00 × 100 = 0.75 % of full scale.
chapters.trap: Never correct a span error with the zero knob, or a zero error with the span knob — adjust zero first, then span, and repeat. Second trap: calling an instrument 'calibrated' when only a verification check was done; a calibration records the deviation, it does not always remove it.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 for what the sensor is converting, so the input and output units are clear.
chapters.leave: The full statistical treatment of uncertainty and repeated readings to Chapter 1.6; bridge and divider circuits used during calibration to Unit 6; display instruments such as DVM and calibrators to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: For an input that is not changing, a sensor is fully described by a small set of numbers — accuracy, precision, resolution, sensitivity, linearity, span, range, hysteresis and drift — and each one answers a different question.
chapters.depth: Give the definition, symbol, formula and unit of each, with the difference stated explicitly. Range and span: range is the two limits (0–250 kPa), span is the difference (250 kPa). Sensitivity S = Δoutput/Δinput, quoted in mV/kPa or mV/V per unit. Accuracy: closeness of the mean reading to the true value, quoted as ± value or ± % of full scale (%FS) or ± % of reading — say clearly which. Error = indicated − true, with bias as the systematic part and precision as the scatter. Precision and repeatability: closeness of repeated readings to each other, quoted as a standard deviation or a band. Resolution: smallest input change that gives a detectable output change; threshold and dead band belong here. Linearity: maximum deviation of the calibration curve from a straight line, expressed as %FS; name terminal-based (end-point), best-fit (least-squares) and independent linearity. Hysteresis: difference between up-scale and down-scale readings at the same input. Drift: slow change with time or temperature. Also tolerance and the difference between %FS and %reading at a low reading. Do not do transducer-specific characteristics here — a strain gauge's gauge factor belongs to Unit 2.

figure.aria: Output against pressure: the straight ideal line of slope 0.2 mV/kPa and the measured curve that sits 0.02 mV above zero and bows up to 0.6 mV away from the line near mid-span.

chapters.example: A 0–250 kPa sensor has a 0–50 mV output. Sensitivity = 50 mV / 250 kPa = 0.2 mV/kPa. Ten readings at a true 100 kPa give a mean of 99.6 kPa with a sample standard deviation of 0.5 kPa. Bias error = 99.6 − 100 = −0.4 kPa = −0.16 %FS. Precision band at 3σ = ±1.5 kPa = ±0.6 %FS. Resolution from the display = 0.1 kPa = 0.04 %FS. Linearity from the calibration curve = 0.6 mV = 3 kPa = 1.2 %FS. Reading: good precision, small bias, mediocre linearity.
chapters.trap: Accuracy and precision are not the same thing — a sensor can be precise and inaccurate by a fixed bias. Second trap: ± %FS and ± %reading differ hugely at low readings (1 %FS on a 0–250 kPa device is ±2.5 kPa at any point; 1 % of a 10 kPa reading is only ±0.1 kPa). Third trap: calling resolution and sensitivity the same; high sensitivity with poor resolution is possible.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.1 and 1.3: the classification terms and the calibration line against which these numbers are measured.
chapters.leave: Gauge factor, bridge sensitivity and load cell characteristics to Unit 2; the behaviour of the same sensor when the input varies with time to Chapter 1.5; combining these errors statistically to Chapter 1.6.

chapters.idea: When the input changes with time the sensor cannot follow it instantly, so it is modelled as a zero, first or second order system whose constants set the lag, the overshoot and the useful frequency range.
chapters.depth: Write the general transfer function H(s) = output(s)/input(s); some syllabi call this the mathematical model of the transducer. Zero order: y = Kx, an ideal instantaneous sensor (a well-loaded potentiometer, a pure resistor divider). First order: τ(dy/dt) + y = Kx, with τ the time constant in seconds; step response y = KA(1 − e^(−t/τ)), so 63.2 % at t = τ, 95 % at t = 3τ, 99 % at t = 5τ; ramp response settles to a constant lag τ × slope; sinusoidal response has amplitude ratio 1/√(1 + (ωτ)²) and phase lag tan⁻¹(ωτ), with bandwidth at ω = 1/τ. Physical example: a thermocouple or thermistor bead with thermal capacity, τ = mc/(hA). Second order: (1/ωn²)(d²y/dt²) + (2ζ/ωn)(dy/dt) + y = Kx, with ωn the undamped natural frequency in rad/s and ζ the damping ratio (dimensionless); mechanical model is mass–spring–damper with ωn = √(k/m) and ζ = c/(2√(km)). Give the step response for ζ < 1 with overshoot Mp = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) and peak time tp = π/ωd, ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²); state the ζ = 1 and ζ > 1 cases briefly. Sinusoidal response: amplitude ratio 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) with r = ω/ωn, resonance near r = √(1 − 2ζ²), sharp only for small ζ. Cover impulse and ramp inputs in one line each. Keep the algebra to the results an exam asks for.

figure.aria: Unit step response of two sensors: the first order curve rising smoothly to 0.63 at 2 s, and the second order curve with 1 Hz natural frequency and damping 0.2 overshooting to about 1.53 before settling.

chapters.example: A thermocouple with τ = 2 s is dipped from 25 °C into a bath at 100 °C. Step size = 100 − 25 = 75 °C. At t = 2 s: T = 25 + 75(1 − e⁻¹) = 25 + 75 × 0.632 = 72.4 °C. At t = 6 s (3τ): T = 25 + 75 × 0.950 = 96.3 °C. If the bath is ramped at 2 °C/s instead of stepped, the reading lags by τ × slope = 2 × 2 = 4 °C. A pressure diaphragm is second order with fn = 1 Hz (ωn = 6.283 rad/s) and ζ = 0.2: overshoot = exp(−π × 0.2/√(1 − 0.04)) = exp(−0.641) = 0.527, i.e. 52.7 %; peak time = π/(6.283 × 0.980) = 0.51 s; 2 % settling ≈ 4/(ζωn) = 4/1.257 = 3.2 s.
chapters.trap: Reading τ as the time to reach the final value — it is the time to reach 63.2 %. Also, the overshoot formula only holds for ζ < 1; do not use it for a critically damped or overdamped system. Third trap: fn given in Hz must be converted with ωn = 2πfn before it enters any formula.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4 for sensitivity K and full scale, and first-order differential equations and complex numbers from mathematics.
chapters.leave: Seismic and accelerometer mechanical design to Unit 4; frequency response of filters and amplifiers to Unit 6; detailed Laplace work to the mathematics course.

chapters.idea: Every reading carries an error, and the honest way to report a result is the best estimate plus an uncertainty built from the systematic errors and the statistics of repeated readings.
chapters.depth: Classify errors: gross or blunder, systematic (bias, calibration offset, scale factor error, loading, drift) and random (noise, vibration, supply ripple). Give absolute error, relative error, percentage error, and the idea of a correction. Explain how systematic and random errors respond differently to averaging: averaging shrinks random scatter but never removes bias. Statistics for a set of n readings: mean x̄ = Σx/n, median, range, sample variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), sample standard deviation s, standard deviation of the mean s/√n, and the confidence interval x̄ ± k·s/√n with k = 1, 2, 3 for roughly 68 %, 95 %, 99 %. Show a histogram and say when the normal distribution is a fair model. Give the propagation rule for combined uncertainty: for y = a + b, u_y = √(u_a² + u_b²); for y = ab or a/b add fractional uncertainties in quadrature; for y = aⁿ multiply the fractional uncertainty by |n|. Mention that the reading resolution contributes a rectangular uncertainty of ± half the last digit, divided by √3 for a standard uncertainty. Also chi-square or least-squares curve fitting in one short section: slope and intercept from a straight-line fit, and the correlation coefficient as a quality check. One line on rejecting an outlier only with a stated rule.

figure.title: Ten readings of a 5.000 V reference
figure.aria: Ten voltage readings with their deviations in millivolts, showing the two most deviant readings at +30 mV and -30 mV and the rest clustered near the mean.

chapters.example: Ten readings of a 5.000 V reference: 5.01, 4.98, 5.02, 4.99, 5.00, 5.03, 4.97, 5.01, 4.99, 5.00 V. Sum = 50.00 V, so x̄ = 5.000 V and the bias is 0.000 V. Deviations in mV: +10, −20, +20, −10, 0, +30, −30, +10, −10, 0; sum of squares = 100 + 400 + 400 + 100 + 0 + 900 + 900 + 100 + 100 + 0 = 3000 mV². s² = 3000/9 = 333.3 mV², s = 18.3 mV. Standard error = 18.3/√10 = 5.8 mV. At 95 % (k = 2): 5.000 V ± 11.6 mV. The display resolves 0.01 V, i.e. ±5 mV rectangular = ±2.9 mV standard, smaller than the scatter, so the scatter dominates.
chapters.trap: Dividing by n instead of n − 1 for a sample standard deviation, which understates s and makes the result look better than it is. Second trap: adding uncertainties arithmetically instead of in quadrature. Third trap: quoting s of a single reading when the question asks for the uncertainty of the mean — that is s/√n.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.4 for bias, precision and resolution, and Chapter 1.3 for the calibration deviation that feeds the systematic uncertainty. Mean and standard deviation from the statistics course.
chapters.leave: Least-squares fitting of a calibration line in full detail to a statistics text; bridge null detection and display instrument accuracy to Unit 6; multi-sensor data fusion and smart sensor self-diagnostics to Unit 5.
